elicitation_input.question: What is the best kind of suspension for an amputee?
elicitation_input.question_type: Request for a list of resources where one can find more information

llm_generation.text:
There is no single “best” suspension for every amputee. The best choice depends on **amputation level, residual-limb shape and skin condition, activity level, sweating, muscle control, and whether the prosthesis is for daily walking, sports, or work**. A certified prosthetist should assess the limb in person—especially if there is pain, skin breakdown, diabetes, poor circulation, or a recent amputation.

## Common suspension options

| Suspension type | Often best suited for | Main advantages | Common drawbacks |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Elevated vacuum suspension** | Active transtibial or transfemoral users; fluctuating limb volume; need for excellent control | Very secure attachment, reduced pistoning, may help manage daily volume changes | More expensive and mechanically complex; requires a good seal, maintenance, and sufficient skin tolerance |
| **Suction suspension** | Transtibial or transfemoral users with a reasonably stable limb and good soft-tissue coverage | Secure, relatively low profile, no external straps | Can be difficult with sweating, volume fluctuation, or an irregular limb; donning may be harder |
| **Seal-in liner / anatomical suspension** | Many below-knee amputees, especially those wanting fewer external components | Comfortable, clean appearance, good suspension without a sleeve in some designs | Requires an appropriate limb shape and intact skin; seal can fail with sweat or volume changes |
| **Pin-locking liner** | New users, people with limited hand strength or dexterity, and many below-knee users | Simple to put on and remove; reliable when correctly fitted | Can cause distal traction or pressure at the end of the limb; may increase pistoning for some users |
| **Lanyard or strap suspension** | People who need easier donning, have a short limb, or cannot tolerate distal pin pressure | Simple and adjustable; useful when suction is impractical | May allow more movement inside the socket and can create pressure or skin shear |
| **Cuff strap or supracondylar suspension** | Some transtibial users with adequate knee anatomy and moderate activity | Simple, durable, and relatively inexpensive | Can irritate the thigh or limit comfort; generally less secure than vacuum or well-fitting suction |
| **Pelvic-band or hip-joint suspension** | Certain transfemoral users, very short residual limbs, or difficult anatomy | Provides extra mechanical security when other systems are inadequate | Bulky, can restrict movement, and may be less comfortable or cosmetically appealing |
| **Osseointegration** | Carefully selected adults with persistent socket intolerance or major socket-related limitations | Direct skeletal attachment eliminates the socket and may improve comfort and control | Major surgery, infection and fracture risks, long rehabilitation, and not appropriate for everyone |

## General practical recommendations

### For a below-knee amputation
- **Most active users:** a well-fitted **seal-in or elevated-vacuum system** is often preferred when the skin can tolerate it.
- **New amputees or people who value easy donning:** a **pin-lock liner** is often a practical starting point.
- **Short residual limb, weak hand function, or difficult anatomy:** a **lanyard, strap, or suction system** may work better than a distal pin.
- **Very sensitive distal tissue:** avoid assuming pin-lock is best; a vacuum, suction, or lanyard design may distribute forces more comfortably.

### For an above-knee amputation
- A **seal-in or suction socket**, often with **elevated vacuum**, can provide excellent control and reduce pistoning.
- People with substantial volume fluctuation may benefit from **vacuum-assisted suspension**, adjustable sockets, or carefully managed liner and sock systems.
- Those with a short residual limb or difficult soft-tissue control may need a **mechanical auxiliary suspension**, such as a pelvic belt or hip-joint system.

## Elevated vacuum versus pin-lock

A common comparison is:

- **Elevated vacuum:** usually better for minimizing pistoning and maintaining contact with the socket during walking; often preferred by active users, but may require approximately **10–30 minutes** of daily maintenance and a good seal.
- **Pin-lock:** usually easier to learn and remove; may be suitable for many users, but some experience distal pulling, discomfort, or increased movement inside the socket.

Neither is automatically superior. A person who walks approximately **3–8 hours per day**, uses uneven terrain, or notices repeated pistoning may gain more from vacuum or suction. A person who needs fast, simple donning and has stable limb volume may do very well with pin-lock.

## Fit matters more than the label

Even the best suspension type will fail if the socket or liner is poorly fitted. Warning signs include:

- Pain that persists for more than approximately **20–30 minutes** after removing the prosthesis
- Redness lasting longer than approximately **20–30 minutes**
- Blisters, open areas, drainage, numbness, or burning
- A feeling
